Below are the five final prompts. Each is self-contained and written for unattended Claude Cowork runs, so you can paste one and walk away. Each one:

- **Reads your repo first** (`dump.txt` if present, `README.md`, existing books, `BookCompiler`/`QuestionCompiler`/`SyntaxHighlighter` source), so the compiler is the source of truth rather than my description of it.
- **Plans, writes to disk, validates, audits, and fixes itself** without asking questions or waiting for "continue", and it can resume if the run is interrupted.
- **Balances timeless and current** with a fixed structure: a timeless core in every section, plus a short, clearly dated "Where this shows up today" block, with a cap on how much quiz material may depend on dated facts.

Each prompt repeats the same shared block (everything before `BOOK SPECIFICATION`), so you can run any of them alone.

WORKFLOW (follow in order)
1. PLAN: write `_build/data-representation-traps/plan.md` with the full table of contents (chapter folder names, section file names, one-line learning goal per section, and the 5–7 question concepts per section so no concept repeats across sections). 3–5 sections per chapter; Chapter 7 may have 3–4 review sections. 2. CREATE `progress.md` as a checklist of every file; tick items as you finish them.

Do not delete `_build/`; the author will do that. Do not modify anything outside `content/books/data-representation-traps/` and `_build/data-representation-traps/`.

HARD FORMAT RULES (verify against the compiler; the compiler wins)
Files:
- `content/books/<slug>/book.yml`: `title`, `author`, `summary`, `date`, `tags`, `draft: false`.
- Chapter folders `NN-chapter-slug/` containing `chapter.yml` (`title`, `summary`, `draft: false`).
- Section files `NN-subchapter-slug.md` inside chapter folders. Names use lowercase letters, digits, and single hyphens only.
Front matter of every section: `title` and `questions` (5–7 questions).
Each question has: `id`, `prompt`, `type`, `explanation`, `options`.
- `id`: unique lowercase slug within the section (letters, digits, hyphens). NEVER `yes`, `no`, `true`, `false`, `null` (any case).
- `type`: ALWAYS present, either `single` (exactly 1 correct option) or `multiple` (2–3 correct options out of 5; the prompt must end with "Select all that apply.").
- `options`: 4–5 items; each has `text`; right answers also have `correct: true`; wrong answers have no `correct` key.
- `explanation`: required on every question and fully self-contained. Structure: (a) why the correct option(s) hold, with the rule or standard behind it; (b) why EACH distractor fails, naming the specific misconception; (c) all arithmetic, bit math, or traces step by step. Refer to options by their text, NEVER by letter or position (e.g., never "option B").
YAML safety:
- Double-quote every string value (`title`, `id`, `prompt`, option `text`, `summary`, etc.). Escape inner double quotes. This avoids boolean/number/null coercion and `: ` / ` #` / leading `` ` `` `@` `[` `{` `*` `- ` problems.
- Long explanations: use a block scalar (`explanation: |-` with indented lines) if the compiler or existing books accept it; otherwise a double-quoted string. Test with the real compiler on the first section before writing the rest.
- Never put `---` at the start of a line inside front matter content.
Markdown body:
- The body starts with `## Learning objectives` (3–5 bullets), then the structure below.
- Every fenced code block has a language tag from this set, intersected with what `SyntaxHighlighter` supports: `csharp`, `python`, `javascript`, `sql`, `bash`, `json`, `yaml`, `html`. Use Markdown tables (not code fences) for bit layouts, packet layouts, and schedules. Keep snippets short and exact; run snippets you are unsure of to confirm their output.
Answer-position balance (the UI does not shuffle): for question number k (1-based) in section number s of the book, place the first correct option at index ((k + s) mod n), 0-based, where n is that question's option count; for `multiple` questions, place correct options at that index and the next valid index(es). validate.py must verify that no position holds more than 40% of the correct answers within any section.

SECTION STRUCTURE (400–1200 words of prose per section, one crisp concept each)
1. `## Learning objectives`
2. `## The invariant` : the timeless mechanism, stated precisely, with the primary-source rule behind it.
3. `## Worked example` : concrete numbers, a trace, or a short code sample with exact expected output.
4. `## Where this shows up today` : the relevance block (see policy below).
5. `## Pitfalls checklist` : 3–6 bullets of mistakes engineers actually make.
6. `## Key takeaways` : 3–5 bullets.

TIMELESS-VS-CURRENT POLICY (apply strictly)
- At least 80% of every section's content, and at least 5 of its 6–7 questions... (more precisely: at most ONE question per section may depend on a fact that could change within five years) must rest on invariants: math, protocol or standard rules, hardware or algorithmic limits.
- The "Where this shows up today" block is at most about 15% of the section. It connects the invariant to how the world looks in 2026: current systems, current incidents or trends, current defaults. Name products only as examples of a mechanism, never as the point.

If you cannot verify a current-state claim, drop it or restate it as a general mechanism. Never guess versions, dates, or adoption figures.
- Citations: cite spec or RFC numbers at document level; add a section number only when you have confirmed it. For paywalled standards, cite the standard and its role without quoting text. Never fabricate a quote, page number, or section number. Distinguish universal standard behavior from language-, engine-, or vendor-specific behavior and label each explicitly.
- Dated facts must never be the only reason an answer is correct; an answer should still be defensible if the product changed.

QUESTION QUALITY RULES
- Mix per section: at least 2 compute-or-trace questions, at least 1 "spot the bug / what does this print" question, and the rest conceptual or scenario-based.
- Distractors are real misconceptions, plausible and parallel in length and style; the correct option must not be systematically the longest.
- No "all of the above" or "none of the above". No trick wording. No negations in stems unless emphasized with NOT.
- Every question must be answerable using only what that section teaches plus the explanation. No concept is tested twice across the whole book except in Chapter 7 (review), which must combine concepts from earlier chapters.
- Prompts are Markdown; use inline code for identifiers and values.

EXEMPLAR (shape only; do not copy its content)
````markdown
---
title: "Integer Division Truncation"
questions:
  - id: "negative-division"
    type: "single"
    prompt: "In C#, what does `-7 / 2` evaluate to?"
    explanation: |-
      C# integer division truncates toward zero, so the exact quotient -3.5 becomes -3.
      "-4" is what floor division would give (as in Python's `//`), but C# does not floor.
      "-3.5" is wrong because both operands are `int`, so the result is `int`.
      "4" ignores the sign entirely.
      Arithmetic: 7 / 2 = 3 remainder 1, so |quotient| = 3; the sign is negative, giving -3.
    options:
      - text: "-4"
      - text: "-3"
        correct: true
      - text: "-3.5"
      - text: "4"
---

## Learning objectives

- Predict the result of integer division for negative operands.

BOOK SPECIFICATION
- Slug: data-representation-traps
- Title: "Data Representation Traps: Floating-Point, Unicode, and Time"
- Summary: "The language-agnostic invariants behind IEEE 754 arithmetic, Unicode encoding and text segmentation, and clocks, calendars, and time zones — and the assumptions that silently break production code."
- Tags: [fundamentals, floating-point, unicode, time, engineering]
- Author/date: author id per Step 0; `date` = 2026-11-27 in the repo's date format.
- Audience: working software engineers (1–15 years experience) who use a mainstream language daily. Prerequisites: binary and hexadecimal notation, basic programming. Examples may use C#, Python, and JavaScript to show that the invariant is language-independent while the surface behavior differs.
- Primary sources to cite where relevant: IEEE 754-2019; The Unicode Standard and UAX #15, UAX #29, UTS #10; IETF RFC 3629, RFC 2781, RFC 3339; ISO 8601; IANA Time Zone Database; POSIX time definitions; Goldberg's "What Every Computer Scientist Should Know About Floating-Point Arithmetic".

Chapters (folder names fixed; choose 3–5 sections for each):
01-binary-floating-point-anatomy: binary32 and binary64 sign/exponent/significand layout, exponent bias (127 and 1023), hidden leading 1, subnormals and gradual underflow, exact bit-pattern-to-value arithmetic, special encodings. Today: low-precision formats in ML and graphics (FP16, bfloat16, FP8) as the same layout idea with fewer bits; verify current hardware or standard status before stating specifics.
02-floating-point-arithmetic-and-traps: why 0.1 + 0.2 != 0.3, round-to-nearest ties-to-even, ULP growth, the 2^53 exact-integer limit, catastrophic cancellation, non-associativity, NaN (payloads, NaN != NaN), +0.0 vs -0.0, infinities, comparison with tolerances, when to use decimal or integer minor units (money). Today: JSON number handling across languages (e.g., large integer IDs in JavaScript), summation strategies (pairwise, Kahan) in numerical libraries.
03-code-points-utf-8-and-utf-16: scalar values vs code points vs code units, UTF-8 prefix bit patterns for 1–4 bytes, self-synchronization, ASCII compatibility, overlong and invalid sequences, BOM pitfalls, UTF-16 surrogates (0xD800–0xDFFF), BMP vs astral planes, byte-count arithmetic. Today: UTF-8 as the dominant interchange encoding; which major languages and runtimes use which internal string representation; `utf8mb4` vs legacy MySQL `utf8`; verify claims.
04-text-length-indexing-normalization-and-sorting: why "length" differs for UTF-8 bytes, UTF-16 units, scalar values, and UAX #29 grapheme clusters; combining marks, ZWJ emoji sequences, regional-indicator flags, skin-tone modifiers; NFC/NFD/NFKC/NFKD; code-point order vs locale collation; case folding traps (Turkish I, German ß); homoglyph and normalization-based security issues (identifier comparison, usernames). Today: ever-growing emoji sequences and why fixed-width assumptions keep failing; verify the current Unicode version before naming it.
05-calendars-epochs-and-clocks: Unix epoch and the 2038 signed 32-bit overflow, Gregorian leap-year rule (4/100/400) with worked cases, UTC vs TAI vs GPS time, leap seconds and smearing, wall-clock vs monotonic clocks and why elapsed time must use monotonic sources, clock skew and NTP step vs slew. Today: the international decision to phase out leap seconds (verify the resolution and its timeline from a primary source), 2038 exposure in embedded and legacy 32-bit systems, distributed-system timestamps.
06-time-zones-dst-and-serialization: fixed offsets vs IANA regions, spring-forward gaps (nonexistent local times), fall-back overlaps (ambiguous local times), storing future scheduled events as local time plus zone vs past events as UTC instants, tzdata changes by governments, ISO 8601 / RFC 3339 profiles, SQL and JSON timestamp pitfalls (naive vs aware types). Today: modern date-time APIs (e.g., .NET `DateTimeOffset` and `TimeProvider`, Java `java.time`, the JavaScript Temporal proposal's status: verify), tzdata update delivery to containers and runtimes.
07-cross-chapter-review-and-diagnostics: scenario debugging that combines floating-point precision, truncation of UTF-8 or UTF-16 mid-sequence, `VARCHAR(N)` byte vs character limits, and time-zone or clock bugs. Each question presents a short realistic bug report or snippet and asks for the root cause or the minimal correct fix.

Deliver the complete book on disk: `book.yml`, every `chapter.yml`, every section `.md` file, with all required content in full and no placeholders or truncation. Begin now with Step 0.

BOOK SPECIFICATION
- Slug: relational-sql-and-transactions
- Title: "Relational Theory, SQL Semantics & Transaction Anomalies"
- Summary: "The timeless mechanics of relational algebra, SQL's logical execution and three-valued logic, B-tree indexing invariants, and MVCC/lock-based transaction isolation levels."
- Tags: [sql, databases, relational-theory, transactions, concurrency]
- Author/date: author id per Step 0; `date` = 2026-11-27 in the repo's date format.
- Audience: working software engineers who write SQL but have never studied the theory. Prerequisites: basic SELECT/JOIN/GROUP BY, general programming. Prefer portable SQL; mark any dialect-specific syntax clearly with the engine name.
- Primary sources to cite where relevant: E.F. Codd (1970); ISO/IEC 9075 (SQL standard); Berenson et al. (1995) "A Critique of ANSI SQL Isolation Levels"; Fekete et al. (2005) and Cahill, Röhm, Fekete (2008) on snapshot isolation and SSI; Comer (1979) "The Ubiquitous B-Tree"; official PostgreSQL, MySQL InnoDB, SQL Server, and SQLite documentation.

Chapters (folder names fixed; choose 3–5 sections for each):
01-relational-foundations-and-normalization: sets vs SQL multisets (bags), superkeys, candidate, primary and foreign keys, functional dependencies, 1NF/2NF/3NF/BCNF with concrete insert, update, and delete anomalies on small tables, lossless decomposition, when controlled denormalization is justified. Today: JSON/document columns in relational engines as a deliberate 1NF trade-off; analytics-oriented denormalized models.
02-sql-logical-query-processing-order: FROM -> JOIN/ON -> WHERE -> GROUP BY -> HAVING -> SELECT -> DISTINCT -> ORDER BY -> LIMIT/OFFSET; why aliases work in ORDER BY but not in WHERE/HAVING (and the dialect exceptions); WHERE vs ON in LEFT OUTER JOIN; EXISTS vs IN vs JOIN and duplicate-multiplication traps; logical order vs physical execution order (the optimizer may reorder if the result is equivalent). Today: CTEs and whether engines inline or materialize them (verify per engine and version).
03-three-valued-logic-and-null-semantics: TRUE/FALSE/UNKNOWN truth tables for AND, OR, NOT; why `WHERE x <> 5` drops NULL rows; why `NOT IN (subquery)` returns nothing when the subquery yields a NULL while `NOT EXISTS` does not; COUNT(*) vs COUNT(col) vs SUM(col) on empty and all-NULL groups; `IS DISTINCT FROM`; NULLs in UNIQUE constraints, GROUP BY, DISTINCT, and ORDER BY across dialects. Today: `UNIQUE NULLS NOT DISTINCT` and engine differences (verify versions).
04-grouping-aggregation-and-window-functions: GROUP BY functional-dependency rule, HAVING vs WHERE, aggregate edge cases, window frames (ROWS vs RANGE vs GROUPS) and the default frame trap, ROW_NUMBER vs RANK vs DENSE_RANK, running totals, top-N per group, gaps and islands. Today: window functions as the standard tool for analytics queries; availability across engines (verify).
05-b-plus-tree-indexes-selectivity-and-joins: B+tree anatomy (fanout, depth arithmetic, linked leaves), composite indexes and the leftmost-prefix rule, sargability (functions on indexed columns, leading wildcards, implicit type conversions), covering indexes and index-only scans, selectivity and the point where a full scan beats an index, nested-loop vs hash vs merge join and when each wins, statistics and cardinality-estimation errors. Today: why hash and LSM-based indexes, columnar storage, and vector indexes are different structures solving different problems (mechanism-level only; verify any named feature).
06-transaction-anomalies-and-isolation-levels: dirty write, dirty read, non-repeatable read, phantom, lost update, read skew, write skew with fully worked interleaved schedules; ANSI SQL-92 levels vs Berenson et al.; two-phase locking vs MVCC vs snapshot isolation vs SSI; `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE`, gap and next-key locks, deadlock formation and detection, retries on serialization failure. 03-udp-quic-and-http3: UDP as message-framed and connectionless; QUIC's stream multiplexing, per-stream loss recovery, connection IDs and migration, 1-RTT and 0-RTT handshakes and replay risk, QUIC's integration with TLS 1.3, why QUIC runs over UDP (middlebox ossification). 04-dns-resolution-and-caching-invariants: root, TLD, authoritative hierarchy; recursive vs iterative resolution; record types (A, AAAA, CNAME, MX, TXT, SRV, NS, PTR, SOA); why a CNAME cannot coexist with other records at the same name (zone apex consequences, ALIAS/ANAME as provider-specific workarounds); positive TTL vs negative caching (SOA minimum, RFC 2308); anycast; DNSSEC basics at the concept level. HARD FORMAT RULES (verify against the compiler; the compiler wins)
Files:
- `content/books/<slug>/book.yml`: `title`, `author`, `summary`, `date`, `tags`, `draft: false`.
- Chapter folders `NN-chapter-slug/` containing `chapter.yml` (`title`, `summary`, `draft: false`).

Front matter of every section: `title` and `questions` (5–7 questions).
Each question has: `id`, `prompt`, `type`, `explanation`, `options`.

- `type`: ALWAYS present, either `single` (exactly 1 correct option) or `multiple` (2–3 correct options out of 5; the prompt must end with "Select all that apply.").
- `options`: 4–5 items; each has `text`; right answers also have `correct: true`; wrong answers have no `correct` key.
- `explanation`: required on every question and fully self-contained. Structure: (a) the exact invariant or attack that makes the correct option(s) true; (b) why EACH distractor is insecure, false, or irrelevant, naming the specific misconception; (c) all XOR, keystream, birthday-bound, or brute-force arithmetic step by step. Refer to options by their text, NEVER by letter or position (e.g., never "option B").
YAML safety:
- Double-quote every string value (`title`, `id`, `prompt`, option `text`, `summary`, etc.). Escape inner double quotes. This avoids boolean/number/null coercion and `: ` / ` #` / leading `` ` `` `@` `[` `{` `*` `- ` problems (e.g., option text `"128"`, `"256"`, `"Yes"`, HTTP header strings containing `: `).
- Long explanations: use a block scalar (`explanation: |-` with indented lines) if the compiler or existing books accept it; otherwise a double-quoted string. Test with the real compiler on the first section before writing the rest.
- Never put `---` at the start of a line inside front matter content.
Markdown body:
- The body starts with `## Learning objectives` (3–5 bullets), then the structure below.
- Every fenced code block has a language tag from this set, intersected with what `SyntaxHighlighter` supports: `csharp`, `python`, `javascript`, `sql`, `bash`, `json`, `yaml`, `html`. Show HTTP headers (CORS, cookies) in `bash` blocks (or Markdown tables) unless the highlighter supports a better tag. Keep snippets short and exact.
Answer-position balance (the UI does not shuffle): for question number k (1-based) in section number s of the book, place the first correct option at index ((k + s) mod n), 0-based, where n is that question's option count; for `multiple` questions, place correct options at that index and the next valid index(es). validate.py must verify that no position holds more than 40% of the correct answers within any section.

SECTION STRUCTURE (400–1200 words of prose per section, one crisp concept each)
1. `## Learning objectives`
2. `## The invariant` : the timeless property or failure mode, stated precisely, with the primary-source basis.
3. `## Worked example` : concrete bytes, numbers, a toy attack trace, or a short code sample with exact expected output.
4. `## Where this shows up today` : the relevance block (see policy below).
5. `## Pitfalls checklist` : 3–6 bullets of mistakes engineers actually make.
6. `## Key takeaways` : 3–5 bullets, including the "use this instead" fix.

TIMELESS-VS-CURRENT POLICY (apply strictly)
- At most ONE question per section may depend on a fact that could change within five years (recommended parameters, browser defaults, standardization status). All other questions must rest on invariants: the math, the definitions of security properties, the attack mechanics, and the specifications' logic.
- The "Where this shows up today" block is at most about 15% of the section. It connects the invariant to how the world looks in 2026: current standards, library defaults, browser behavior, incident patterns. Every dated claim must be written as "As of November 2026, ..." and, if it names a library, standard, or version, include it. Name products only as examples of a mechanism, never as the point.

Never fabricate a quote, table value, or parameter. Distinguish what is proven (mathematical), what is standardized, and what is merely common practice.

QUESTION QUALITY RULES
- Mix per section: at least 2 compute-or-trace questions, at least 1 "what is wrong with this design/snippet" question, and the rest conceptual or scenario-based.
- Distractors are real misconceptions, plausible and parallel in length and style; the correct option must not be systematically the longest.

- Prompts are Markdown; use inline code for identifiers and values.

EXEMPLAR (shape only; do not copy its content)
````markdown
---
title: "Integer Division Truncation"
questions:
  - id: "negative-division"
    type: "single"
    prompt: "In C#, what does `-7 / 2` evaluate to?"
    explanation: |-
      C# integer division truncates toward zero, so the exact quotient -3.5 becomes -3.
      "-4" is what floor division would give (as in Python's `//`), but C# does not floor.
      "-3.5" is wrong because both operands are `int`, so the result is `int`.
      "4" ignores the sign entirely.
      Arithmetic: 7 / 2 = 3 remainder 1, so |quotient| = 3; the sign is negative, giving -3.
    options:
      - text: "-4"
      - text: "-3"
        correct: true
      - text: "-3.5"
      - text: "4"
---

## Learning objectives

- Predict the result of integer division for negative operands.

Chapters (folder names fixed; choose 3–5 sections for each):
01-threat-models-entropy-and-timing-leaks: Kerckhoffs's principle, defining the attacker, CSPRNG vs non-cryptographic PRNG (`Random` vs `RandomNumberGenerator`, `secrets`, `crypto.getRandomValues`), seeds and entropy, brute-force bit-security arithmetic (128-bit vs 256-bit), why string `==` leaks via timing and how constant-time comparison works (e.g., `CryptographicOperations.FixedTimeEquals`, `hmac.compare_digest`). Today: OS-provided randomness as the default source; why home-grown randomness and seeded `Random` for tokens keep appearing in incident reports (verify any named incident or omit).
02-symmetric-encryption-and-mode-failures: block vs stream ciphers; ECB structure leakage; CBC with predictable IVs and padding oracles (conceptual explanation, no weaponized code); CTR as a keystream and nonce reuse giving `C1 XOR C2 = P1 XOR P2` with a toy byte example; malleability and bit-flipping on unauthenticated ciphertext; why encryption alone is not integrity. Today: authenticated encryption as the default API in modern libraries and why raw-mode APIs are being discouraged (verify per library).
03-hashes-macs-and-birthday-bounds: preimage, second-preimage, and collision resistance; birthday paradox arithmetic (n-bit hash gives about n/2-bit collision security; the 96-bit random GCM nonce collision bound); length extension on Merkle–Damgård hashes (SHA-256) vs HMAC and SHA-3; Encrypt-then-MAC vs MAC-then-Encrypt; AEAD (AES-GCM, ChaCha20-Poly1305) and the catastrophic effect of GCM nonce reuse (confidentiality and authenticity, GHASH key recovery at concept level); nonce-misuse-resistant constructions at concept level. 04-asymmetric-primitives-and-key-exchange: symmetric vs asymmetric roles and hybrid or envelope encryption; Diffie–Hellman and ECDHE and why unauthenticated DH falls to a man-in-the-middle; signatures vs MACs; why textbook RSA fails (determinism, malleability) and why OAEP and PSS padding matter; forward secrecy; key sizes and equivalent strengths (cite NIST SP 800-57); Grover vs Shor at a high level. 05-password-storage-and-key-derivation: why fast hashes (SHA-256/512), even salted, are wrong for passwords (GPU/ASIC rates with arithmetic); per-user random salts vs rainbow tables; peppers and their limits; work factors and memory-hard KDFs (PBKDF2, bcrypt, scrypt, Argon2id per RFC 9106); HKDF for key expansion vs password hashing; password-hash upgrade-on-login migration. Today: current recommended parameter ranges from OWASP and library docs (verify and state the date and source), passkeys/WebAuthn as phishing-resistant authentication that removes shared secrets (verify status).
06-web-security-invariants: same-origin policy and the origin tuple (scheme, host, port) with surprises (subdomains, cookies ignoring ports and schemes in practice, `document.domain` deprecation: verify); CORS (what it enforces, simple vs preflighted requests, why `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *` cannot be combined with credentials, why CORS is not a server-side authorization boundary); CSRF vs XSS (what CSRF tokens stop, why XSS defeats them, what `HttpOnly` does and does not protect); cookie attributes `Secure`, `HttpOnly`, `SameSite` (Strict, Lax, None) and cookie prefixes; JWT pitfalls (`alg: none`, algorithm confusion, token storage).
